```{r setup, include=FALSE}
set.seed(20260512)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
library(shieldR)
```

A reproducible experiment needs a declared endpoint, a comparison design, a
replication schedule and an explicit multiplicity family. This tutorial shows
those decisions using neutral teaching inputs. It does not reproduce the SHIELD
manuscript or provide calibrated scenario assumptions.

## Define the experiment before looking at outcomes

The unit of analysis is an independently simulated cohort. Patients within a
cohort share queues, vehicles, observations and disruption_risk history, so they are not
independent statistical replicates. Use cohort-level outcomes for the functions
below.

```{r analysis-plan}
master_seed <- 20260512L
scenario <- example_scenario("constrained", N = 6L)
policies <- c("P0", "P1", "P3")
arm_seeds <- setNames(master_seed + seq_along(policies) - 1L, policies)
n_rep <- 6L
bootstrap_resamples <- 10000L
endpoint <- "surv_stage2"
comparison_family <- "teaching-policy-comparisons-at-Stage2"
data.frame(policy = policies, seed = unname(arm_seeds), n_rep = n_rep)
```

The master seed is 20260512. Different arms receive documented, distinct seeds
derived from it. Six replications keep this vignette small; choose the study
replication count using a prospective Monte Carlo precision assessment. The
bootstrap uses the full reporting default of 10,000 resamples. A smaller
bootstrap count may be useful for an interactive preview but must be identified
as such and replaced for a final analysis.

The primary SHIELD endpoint is overall survival as operationalized here by
arrival alive at Stage 2 by the administrative horizon. This is a proportion of
the original cohort, not a Kaplan-Meier survival probability at an arbitrary
time. A patient still alive elsewhere at the horizon is an endpoint failure.
Arrival is recorded before unloading and ends physiological hazard; transport
can continue to Stage 3. Downstream disruptions can still affect the Stage 3 endpoint.

## Run independent policy arms

```{r independent-arms}
arms <- setNames(lapply(policies, function(policy) {
  simulate_shield(scenario, policy = policy, disruption_model = "static",
                  n_rep = n_rep, seed = arm_seeds[[policy]])
}), policies)
summary_P0 <- summarize_shield(arms$P0)
summary_P0[summary_P0$endpoint %in%
             c("surv_stage2", "t_stage2_med", "util_L4", "n_pending"), ]
```

Each row in an arm is one replication; each row above describes an endpoint
across those replications. The medians and quartiles do not describe the
parameter distribution or uncertainty about the model's scientific validity.

```{r endpoint-plot, fig.cap="Neutral teaching run: cohort-level Stage 2 arrival-alive proportions by policy."}
plot(stats::ecdf(arms$P0[[endpoint]]), verticals = TRUE, do.points = FALSE,
     xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Proportion arriving alive at Stage 2",
     ylab = "Cumulative proportion of cohort replications", main = "")
lines(stats::ecdf(arms$P1[[endpoint]]), verticals = TRUE, do.points = FALSE,
      lty = 2)
lines(stats::ecdf(arms$P3[[endpoint]]), verticals = TRUE, do.points = FALSE,
      lty = 3)
legend("bottomright", legend = policies, lty = 1:3, bty = "n")
```

The neutral scenario has zero exposure and physiological hazards. Differences
in arrival outcomes can reflect congestion or the administrative horizon.
The plot is a teaching output and establishes no policy advantage in practice.

## Report nonparametric comparisons in full

`compare_policies()` applies a two-sided, tie-corrected Mann-Whitney U
approximation to independent arms. The test compares distributions; it is not
specifically a test of medians. It also returns Cliff's delta and the difference
in medians with percentile bootstrap 95% intervals. This is a primary
nonparametric framework, with no preliminary normality test.

```{r independent-comparisons}
comparisons <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("P1", "P3"), function(policy) {
  compare_policies(
    arms[[policy]][[endpoint]], arms$P0[[endpoint]],
    label_x = policy, label_y = "P0", family = comparison_family,
    B = bootstrap_resamples, seed = master_seed
  )
}))
comparisons[c("arm_x", "arm_y", "n_x", "n_y", "U", "p_raw_log10",
              "cliff_delta", "cliff_lwr", "cliff_upr",
              "med_diff", "med_diff_lwr", "med_diff_upr",
              "med_diff_ci_degenerate")]
```

Effects are oriented as `x` minus `y`. Positive values favor `x` for survival;
for delay or resource use, whether larger values are desirable depends on the
question. Do not infer direction from the policy labels alone. Cliff's delta
contrasts the probabilities of a randomly drawn `x` exceeding or falling below
a randomly drawn `y`, accounting for ties.

Retain sample sizes, median/IQR descriptives, the U statistic, raw and adjusted
p-values, effect estimates and intervals in the analysis output. The bootstrap
intervals quantify Monte Carlo sampling uncertainty conditional on the model.
They do not include parameter uncertainty, structural uncertainty, measurement
validity or uncertainty from choosing a model after seeing the result.

A bootstrap interval can collapse on this discrete endpoint. Inspect the
`med_diff_ci_degenerate` flag and the interval endpoints; a point interval is
not evidence of empirical certainty.

### Declare the complete FDR family

The family below contains both planned policy contrasts at the same endpoint.
Adjust its complete set of p-values together. If a study defines additional
endpoints or scenarios in the same family, include them before adjustment.
Selecting only significant or interesting contrasts changes the family.

```{r multiplicity}
comparisons$p_bh_log10 <- adjust_fdr(comparisons$p_raw_log10)
comparisons[c("family", "arm_x", "arm_y", "p_raw_log10", "p_bh_log10")]
```

The helpers retain base-10 log p-values so extreme tails remain distinguishable.
`p_raw_log10` is authoritative when a linear p-value underflows; use log
probabilities or a properly formatted bound instead of reporting a computed
probability as zero. `adjust_fdr()` implements Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment for
one supplied family and leaves missing entries missing. It does not infer a
hypothesis grid or silently pool separate families.

### More than two arms

For a prespecified omnibus comparison, use Kruskal-Wallis and retain its H
statistic and degrees of freedom. Any decision to gate pairwise contrasts on
that omnibus result belongs to the declared study analysis plan.

```{r omnibus}
values <- unlist(lapply(arms, `[[`, endpoint), use.names = FALSE)
groups <- rep(names(arms), vapply(arms, nrow, integer(1)))
compare_multiple(values, groups, family = "teaching-omnibus-at-Stage2")
```

The omnibus helper reports the test statistic and p-value. Pairwise effect
sizes and their intervals come from explicitly chosen contrasts; the function
does not select post-hoc comparisons or manufacture a multi-arm effect size.
For association questions, the study's primary nonparametric choice is Spearman;
specify the variables, independent unit and any bootstrap interval separately.

## Paired disruptions-disabled intervention

A paired intervention is a different design. It requires identical parameters,
policy, disruption_risk-response family, replication count and seed schedule, with disruption
enablement as the only changed setting. Clinical draws are indexed by patient
and minute and use a stream separate from policy and disruption draws.

```{r paired-intervention}
with_disruptions <- simulate_shield(
  scenario, policy = "P3", disruption_model = "adaptive", n_rep = n_rep,
  seed = master_seed, disruptions_enabled = TRUE
)
without_disruptions <- simulate_shield(
  scenario, policy = "P3", disruption_model = "adaptive", n_rep = n_rep,
  seed = master_seed, disruptions_enabled = FALSE
)
compare_intervention(with_disruptions, without_disruptions,
                     B = bootstrap_resamples, seed = master_seed)
```

The contrast is **no disruptions minus disruptions**, estimated as a paired mean
difference of cohort proportions with a paired percentile bootstrap interval.
Pair indices are resampled jointly. The helper checks matching identities and
aligns rows by replication identifier.

The neutral exposure is zero, so the intervention has no effect here. In a
user-specified disruption_risk experiment, this is a total modelled intervention effect,
including downstream decisions and administrative-horizon effects. It is not
identical to `n_att_fatal` or a count of direct disruption deaths. Matched arms must
not be passed to the independent-arm Mann-Whitney U helper.

## Preserve missing outcomes and replay the experiment

Arrival-time medians are conditional on arrival. If an arm contains an
undefined median, `compare_policies()` rejects that nonfinite input. Decide
prospectively whether a comparison of defined cohort medians is meaningful,
report the missing counts by arm, and keep the survival/arrival endpoint
alongside it. Replacing a missing time by zero or the horizon changes the
estimand.

Simulation and bootstrap calls restore the caller's RNG state and kind, while
recording their own reproducible configuration. Repeating a run with the same
parameters, software and seeds reproduces its cohort results:

```{r replay}
state_before <- .Random.seed
replayed <- simulate_shield(scenario, policy = "P0", disruption_model = "static",
                           n_rep = n_rep, seed = arm_seeds[["P0"]])
stopifnot(identical(arms$P0, replayed),
          identical(state_before, .Random.seed))
```

### Replay one cohort or distribute a fixed schedule

Use `replication_seeds()` to construct the complete cell schedule once, then
send individual seeds to `simulate_replication()` from your analysis scheduler.
The latter takes a replication seed directly; it does not sample a new cell
schedule or attach study identifiers. Checkpoint naming and workload allocation
remain the analysis project's responsibility.

```{r individual-replication}
schedule <- replication_seeds(n_rep = n_rep, seed = arm_seeds[["P0"]])
stopifnot(identical(schedule, arms$P0$replicate_seed))
first_cohort <- simulate_replication(
  scenario, policy = "P0", disruption_model = "static",
  replication_seed = schedule[1]
)
stopifnot(all(vapply(names(first_cohort), function(column) {
  identical(first_cohort[[column]], arms$P0[[column]][1])
}, logical(1))))
```

Generate the declared full schedule before splitting into chunks. Restarting a
master seed independently for each chunk repeats the beginning of the schedule
and creates duplicate replications. For an disruptions-disabled pair, use the same
schedule in both configurations. Preserve the total replication count and the
mapping from each seed to its replication identifier in durable checkpoints.

For analysis pipelines that already manage their own data frames,
`mann_whitney_u()` exposes the tested U calculation and log tail probability,
`bootstrap_statistic()` exposes named independent or paired interval estimators,
and `effect_magnitude()` provides descriptive Cliff's delta labels. These
primitives do not establish independence or pairing for the caller; prefer the
higher-level comparison functions when using complete run objects.

### Save the complete request

Save the request, full result object, analysis settings and session information.
An RDS retains attributes required for pairing, whereas CSV retains only table
columns.

```{r reproducibility-bundle}
request <- list(parameters = scenario, policy = "P0", disruption_model = "static",
                n_rep = n_rep, seed = arm_seeds[["P0"]])
bundle <- list(request = request, run = arms$P0,
               analysis = list(endpoint = endpoint,
                               family = comparison_family,
                               bootstrap_resamples = bootstrap_resamples,
                               master_seed = master_seed),
               session_info = sessionInfo())
bundle_file <- tempfile("shieldR-study-", fileext = ".rds")
saveRDS(bundle, bundle_file)
restored <- readRDS(bundle_file)
stopifnot(identical(do.call(simulate_shield, restored$request), restored$run))
```

For a real analysis, use a named output directory and retain an immutable copy
of the exact source archive or package commit, the scenario input hash, seed
schedule, replication counts and an environment lockfile. A version number
alone cannot distinguish two uncommitted source states with the same version.
Study scheduling, frozen input/output manifests and publication exports remain
in the analysis project. Method changes require explicit validation before adoption by a study.

```{r session-information}
sessionInfo()
```
